p.seg: "Xìng" (幸, Imperial Visit) means "appropriate to favor."
The common people consider "xìng" (幸) to mean "good fortune."
When the Son of Heaven's carriages arrive,
the officials and people are blessed by his virtue, thus gaining good fortune,
therefore it is called "xìng" (幸).
According to the late emperor's practice,
when he arrived, he would meet with the senior officials, the elders, and the local officials.
He would personally stand at the carriage's railing,
make music,
and bestow food, black silk, Yuè (越) scarves, knives, jade ornaments, and belts.
The people's ranks of nobility were numbered.
Some were granted half of their land tax.
This is why it is called "xìng" (幸),
because they all obtained something they did not deserve.
Wáng Zhòngrèn (王仲任) said:
"The superior man has no luck, but has misfortune;
the petty man has luck, but no misfortune."
The *Chūnqiū Zhuàn* (春秋傳) says:
"When the people have much luck,
it is the country's misfortune."
It speaks of the people obtaining what they do not deserve,
therefore it is called "xìng" (幸).
Therefore, the ruler must be careful in what he favors.
Yù (御), means to advance or draw near.
Generally, clothes put on the body, food and drink put into the mouth, and concubines entering the bedchamber
are all called yù (御).
Those who are loved dearly are all called xìng (幸).
Cèshū (策書),
cè (策) means jiǎn (簡), or simple writing.
The *Lǐjì* (禮記) says:
"If it is not longer than one hundred *zhàng* (丈),
it is not written on *cè* (策)."
call it *tiānjiā* (the imperial family).
*Jìnzhōng* (forbidden palace) refers to the gates and households being forbidden,
those who are not attendants are not allowed to enter,
therefore it is called *jìnzhōng*.
The father of Empress Xiào Yuán, Grand General (*Dà Sīmǎ*) and Marquis of Yángpíng, was named Jìn,
at that time it was avoided,
therefore it was called "Shěng Zhōng" (省中, the Inner Palace).
Now it should be changed,
but afterwards no one spoke of it.
"Xǐ" (璽, Imperial Seal) means "seal",
and "seal" means "trust."
The Son of Heaven's seal has a jade dragon-tiger handle.
In ancient times, both the noble and the humble used it.
The *Yuè Lìng* (月令, Monthly Ordinances) says:
"Secure the sealing seal."
The *Chūnqiū Zuǒshì Zhuàn* (春秋左氏傳, Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals) says:
"When Duke Xiāng of Lǔ (魯襄公) was in Chǔ (楚),
Jì Wǔzǐ (季武子) sent Gōngyě (公冶) to ask,
and a sealed letter was chased and given to him."
This shows that the seals of feudal lords and grand officers were also called "xǐ" (璽).
Wèi Hóng (衛宏) said:
"Before the Qín (秦) dynasty,
the common people all used gold and jade for seals,
with dragon and tiger handles, according to their liking.
However, since the Qín dynasty, only the Son of Heaven calls his seal 'xǐ' (璽),
and only uses jade,
and no officials dare to use it."
daring not to disrespectfully mention the honored title,
which is the meaning of honoring the king.
Chéngyú comes from the law.
The law says, "Whoever dares to steal the Emperor's carriage or clothing."
It refers to what the Emperor wears and eats.
The Emperor is the most honored,
and I dare not profanely mention him,
therefore it is entrusted to the *shèngyú*.
*Shèng* means to carry,
*yú* means carriage.
The Son of Heaven regards the world as his home,
and does not consider the capital's palaces as a permanent dwelling,
therefore he should ride in carriages to travel the world.
Therefore, the ministers entrust the *shèngyú* to speak of him.
Some call it *chējià* (imperial equipage).
The Son of Heaven refers to himself as *xíngzàisuǒ* (where the emperor is residing),
which is like saying that even though I am now in the capital, it is only where I am traveling to.
When touring the realm,
all places where affairs are reported become palaces.
In the capital, it is said to be reporting at *Cháng'ān* Palace,
at Mount Tài it is said to be reporting at *Fènggāo* Palace.
It depends on the location at the time.
Sometimes it is called the court (*cháotíng*),
which also vaguely refers to the place where the honored one is staying,
linking and mentioning the court to speak of it.
Close attendants are called *dàgū* (master);
the many officials and minor officials,
*Zhèn* means "I."
In ancient times, both the honored and the lowly used it;
the noble and the base did not avoid it,
thus it was a title that could be shared.
Yáo called himself *zhèn*,
reigning for seventy years.
Gāo Yáo speaking to Emperor Shùn said, "Zhèn's words are beneficial and can be carried out."
Qū Yuán said "Zhèn huáng kǎo",
this is its meaning.
By the time of Qín,
the Emperor alone used it as a title,
and the Hàn dynasty followed this without change.
Bìxià, refers to the steps,
the place where one ascends to the hall.
The Emperor must have close officials,
holding weapons and stationed at the side of the steps to guard against the unexpected.
The reason for calling it "Bìxià" is that
when officials speak to the Emperor,
they dare not directly point at the Emperor,
therefore, they call out to those at the steps and inform them.
This is the meaning of conveying respect by addressing those nearby.
When submitting memorials, it is also done in this way.
And when officials and commoners speak among themselves, terms such as diànxià, géxià, zúxià, shìzhě, zhíshì, etc. all belong to this category.
Shàng refers to where the honored position is.
Tài shǐ lìng Sīmǎ Qiān, when recording events,
when he should mention the Emperor, he vaguely referred to "Shàng",
The Wáng (王) is the supreme one,
a different name for the four titles.
Wáng (王) is what is used within the capital region.
The Wáng (王) possesses all under heaven,
therefore is called Wáng (王).
*Tiānwáng* is what the various *Xià* states call him;
all under heaven turns towards him,
therefore he is called *tiānwáng*.
*Tiānzǐ* is what the *Yídí* barbarians call him;
he takes Heaven as his father and Earth as his mother,
therefore he is called *tiānzǐ*.
*Tiānjiā* is what the various officials and petty officers call him;
to the *tiānzǐ* there is no outside,
he considers all under Heaven as his family,
therefore he is called *tiānjiā*.
*Tiānzǐ* is a different name for the proper appellation.
*Huángdì* is a title of supreme nobility.
*Huáng* means radiant;
his magnificent virtue shines brightly,
illuminating all without exception.
*Dì* means to examine carefully.
He is able to enact the way of Heaven,
carefully and meticulously attending to the affairs of Heaven,
therefore he is called *huángdì*.
The Hàn (漢) emperor's formal title was "Huángdì" (皇帝),
he referred to himself as "Zhèn" (朕),
ministers and commoners addressed him as "Bìxià" (陛下),
his pronouncements were called "Zhì Zhào" (制詔),
and the official historian's records referred to him as "Shàng" (上).
His carriages, horses, clothing, equipment, and all other items were called "Shèngyú" (乘輿),
his location was called "Xíngzài Suǒ" (行在所),
his residence was called "Jìnzhōng" (禁中),
and the inner palace was called "Shěngzhōng" (省中).
His seal was called "Xǐ" (璽),
his arrival was called "Xìng" (幸),
and what was presented to him was called "Yù" (御).
His commands were categorized as follows: first, "Cèshū" (策書);
second, "Zhìshū" (制書);
third, "Zhàoshū" (詔書);
fourth, "Jièshū" (戒書).
Huángdì (皇帝), Huáng (皇), Wánghòu (王后), and Dì (帝) are all rulers.
In high antiquity, the sons of heaven Páo Xī Shì (庖犧氏) and Shénnóng Shì (神農氏) were called Huáng (皇).
Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜) were called Dì (帝).
The Xià (夏), Yīn (殷), and Zhōu (周) dynasties were called Wáng (王).
The Qín (秦) dynasty, succeeding the end of the Zhōu (周), drove away enemies for the Hàn (漢).
It considered its virtue to encompass the Three Sovereigns (三皇),
and its achievements to include the Five Emperors (五帝).
Therefore, it combined these titles into one.
Emperor Gāo Zǔ (高祖) of Hàn received the mandate,
his merit and virtue were fitting.
Therefore, he followed this usage without change.
Their standard length is two *chǐ* (尺),
shorter ones are half that length.
The next type is one long and one short.
Two strips are bound together with seal script attached below,
starting with the year, month, and day.
It refers to the emperor as "Emperor,"
and is used to command the various princes, kings, and the Three Dukes.
When the various princes, kings, and Three Dukes die in office,
*cèshū* (策書) are also used to eulogize and posthumously name their conduct and bestow them.
These are like the *cè* (策) for the princes.
When the Three Dukes are dismissed due to crimes,
they are also given *cèwén* (策文),
the format being like the above *cè* (策),
but in clerical script, with one *chǐ* (尺),
and one piece of wood with two lines;
only this is different.
Zhìshū (制書) are imperial edicts of decree.
Their text reads "imperial decree."
Edicts of pardon and redemption for the Three Dukes belong to this category.
Accusations and reports by provincial governors (*cìshǐ* 刺史) and commandery administrators (*tàishǒu* 太守), as well as documents submitted downward and requests for transfer, are also like this.
If they are being summoned to become one of the Nine Ministers,
If [someone] is transferred to the capital,
the close officials, then the reporting officials will state their names in full.
If they are dismissed or have committed a crime, their names are omitted.
Whenever an imperial decree is issued, with the seal and official warrant dispatched,
both near and far [officials] seal [the documents] with the imperial seal.
The Shàngshū Lìng seals [it] again with his own seal.
Only for amnesty decrees and redemption decrees are the Sāngōng summoned to the imperial court to receive the imperial decree.
The Sītú seals [it] and sends it openly to the prefectures and counties.
*Zhàoshū* (詔書), means *zhàogào* (詔誥),
and there are three types.
The text of which says:
"Announce to such-and-such official."
The official shall act as before.
This is called *zhàoshū*.
If officials have a memorial to submit,
the Shàngshū Lìng presents it.
Below, there is an edict that says:
"The Emperor responds, saying, 'Approved.'"
If [the edict] is issued to such-and-such official, saying such-and-such, it is also called *zhàoshū*.
If officials have a memorial to submit,
without the Shàngshū Lìng presenting the words of the edict,
then the response says, "Already presented."
The document goes to the appropriate official of the present office.
It is also called *zhào*.
*Jièshū* (戒書) and *jièchì* (戒敕) are [instructions] to the provincial governors (*cìshǐ*, 刺史), commandery administrators (*tàishǒu*, 太守), and the garrison officers on the three borders.
The text of the instruction says, "There is an imperial command to such-and-such official."
This is called a jiè chì (戒敕), an admonition or instruction.
The world generally calls this a cè shū (策書),
which is far from the truth.
Generally, there are four names for documents submitted by officials to the emperor:
one is zhāng (章),
two is zòu (奏),
three is biǎo (表),
and four is bó yì (駮議).
A zhāng (章) requires bowing the head
and is called "bowing head to submit a letter, thanking for grace, reporting matters to reach the palace."
A zòu (奏) also requires bowing the head;
officials in the capital only say "bowing the head,"
and at the end say "bowing the head to report."
If it contains requests or impeachment cases concerning the law against public offices,
it is sent to the Yùshǐ tái (御史臺);
for high officials and military commanders,
it is sent to the Yèzhě tái (謁者臺).
A biǎo (表) does not require bowing the head;
it begins with "Your subject, so-and-so, says,"
and ends with "Your subject, so-and-so, is truly fearful and apprehensive,
bowing head, bowing head,
deserving of death, deserving of death."
On the lower left side, it is attached with "So-and-so official, your subject, so-and-so, submits,"
usually written in two columns if the text is long,
and in five columns if the text is short,
and it is submitted through the Shàngshū (尚書).
Dukes, ministers, commanders, and generals did not state their surnames;
officials below the rank of grand master who shared surnames with other officials differentiated themselves by stating their surnames.
Memorials were called "bào wén" (報聞, reports).

Dukes and ministers would have an usher bring grand masters and those below them, down to clerks and commoners, to the Left Vice Director of the Ministry to report. If it was approved, they would "bào kě" (報可, report approval).
For memorials and documents, the reply "bào yǐ zòu rú shū" (報已奏如書, reported and presented as written) was used.
All memorials and documents were to be opened.
Matters involving secrets
could be placed in a black bag.
For matters involving doubts,
dukes, ministers, and all officials would hold a conference.
If the imperial secretariat or other departments had already made a decision, but one insisted on a different opinion, it was called "bó yì" (駮議, dissenting opinion).
A dissenting opinion stated: "Official X, Y Jiǎ (甲), believes it should be such and such."
Below, it would state: "Your subject, being foolish and obtuse, proposes a different opinion."
If it was not a dissenting opinion,
one would not say "proposes a different opinion."
If it agreed with the emperor's intention,
the official reply would state: "Official X, Y Jiǎ (甲), believes it is acceptable" (mǒu guān mǒu jiǎ yì kě 某官某甲議可).
The Hàn (漢) dynasty inherited the laws of the Qín (秦) dynasty.
When ministers submitted memorials, they all used the phrase "mèi sǐ yán" (昧死言, speaking in disregard of death).
When Wáng Mǎng (王莽) usurped the throne,
he admired ancient customs,
and abolished "mèi sǐ" (昧死),
and used "qǐ shǒu" (稽首, kowtow).
Guāngwǔ (光武) followed this and did not change it.
Court officials said "qǐ shǒu dùn shǒu" (稽首頓首, kowtow and prostrate),
non-court officials said "qǐ shǒu zài bài" (稽首再拜, kowtow and bow twice).
Dukes, ministers, attendants, and directors of the ministry who wore silk to court were called "cháo chén" (朝臣, court officials).
The xiàowèi (校尉), jiàng (將), dàfū (大夫), and those below in the various military camps are also considered court officials.
These are alternate names for the king's personal care and nurturing (lín fǔ 臨撫).
The Son of Heaven calls his people zhàomín (兆民).
The feudal lords call their people wànmín (萬民).
The head of a household with one hundred chariots calls his people bǎixìng (百姓).
The place where the Son of Heaven has his capital is called jīngshī (京師).
Jīng (京) means water (shuǐ 水).
Among the things under the ground, nothing is more numerous than water.
Among the things above the ground, nothing is more numerous than people.
Jīng (京) means great (dà 大).
Shī (師) means multitude (zhòng 眾).
Therefore, it is called jīngshī (京師).
Jīngshī (京師) is the Son of Heaven's territory within a thousand *lǐ*,
symbolizing the sun and moon.
The sun and moon traverse a sequence of a thousand *lǐ*.
These are alternate names for the Son of Heaven's commands.
One is called mìng (命).
Two is called lìng (令).
Three is called zhèng (政).
The Son of Heaven serves Heaven as a father,
serves Earth as a mother,
serves the Sun as an elder brother,
serves the Moon as an elder sister,
and always at the spring equinox, he worships the sun outside the eastern gate,
showing what should be revered,
This instructs the people on the way to serve the ruler.
In the autumn evening, they paid homage to the moon outside the west gate,
distinguishing the meanings of *yīn* and *yáng*.
The Son of Heaven treated the three elders (*sān lǎo*) as fathers,
fitting in with Heaven, Earth, and Man.
He treated the five experienced officials (*wǔ gēng*) as elder brothers,
instructing them about the five ranks of nobility.
*Gēng* means experienced and senior.
*Gēng* refers to the five who alternately arrive.
It also refers to the ability to change oneself for the better through good principles.
Furthermore, concerning the three elders (*sān lǎo*),
*lǎo* means long-lasting, old, and longevity.
All selected those with complete first wives, sons, and daughters.
In ancient times, the Son of Heaven personally bared his arms to cut the sacrificial animal,
held the sauce, and presented the offerings.
The three dukes (*sān gōng*) set up the low tables,
the nine ministers (*jiǔ qīng*) straightened their shoes.
Messengers in comfortable carriages with soft wheels escorted them to and from their homes.
The Son of Heaven alone bowed before the screen.
The following morning, the three elders (*sān lǎo*) went to the palace gate to offer thanks,
because they felt the ceremony was excessively generous.
Also, the five experienced officials (*wǔ gēng*) were sometimes called *sǒu*,
*sǒu* is an elderly term,
with the same meaning as the three elders (*sān lǎo*).
The different names for establishing the new year by the Three Dynasties:
The Xià dynasty used the thirteenth month as the first month,
Ten inches make a chi (尺, chǐ, a unit of length).
The Lü (律, musical pitch) corresponding to the Zhōng Dà Cuò (大蔟)
indicates that all things begin to cluster and grow;
therefore, it is taken as the first month.
The Yin dynasty took the twelfth month as the first month,
and nine inches as a chi.
The Lü corresponding to Dà Lǚ (大呂)
indicates that the yin qi (陰氣) is greatly ascendant,
assisting the Huáng Zhōng (黃鍾) in disseminating qi (氣) and causing all things to grow;
therefore, it is taken as the first month.
The Zhou dynasty took the eleventh month as the first month,
and eight inches as a chi.
The Lü corresponding to Huáng Zhōng (黃鍾)
indicates that the yang qi (陽氣) rises from the Yellow Springs;
therefore, it is taken as the first month.
Different names for the year in the Three Dynasties:
Táng (唐) and Yú (虞) called it zài (載).
Zài (載) means suì (歲), year,
expressing that one year covers and supports everything;
therefore, it is called zài (載).
The Xia dynasty called it suì (歲),
and also rén (稔).
The Shang dynasty called it sì (祀),
the Zhou dynasty called it nián (年).
A leap month is used to compensate for the reduced days of short months
in order to correct the number of days in a year.
Therefore, every three years there is one intercalary month,
and every five years there are two intercalary months.
Different titles for the Son of Heaven, feudal lords, empresses, and wives:
The Son of Heaven's consort is called *hòu*,
*hòu* means "to be behind."
A feudal lord's consort is called *fūrén*,
*fū* means "to support."
A high official's wife is called *rúrén*,
*rú* means "belonging."
A scholar's wife is called *fùrén*,
*fù* means "to submit."
A commoner's wife is called *qī*,
*qī* means "equal."
Dukes and marquises have *fūrén*, *shìfù*, *qī*, and concubines.
An empress has a red ribbon and a jade seal,
a high-ranking consort has a green ribbon and a gold seal,
the color of the green ribbon resembles green.
The Son of Heaven and empress establish different titles for the six palaces:
Three *fū rén*. Emperor Kù had four consorts, symbolizing the four stars of the consorts,
the brightest of which was the principal consort,
and the other three were secondary consorts.
Nine *pín*. The Xià dynasty added three times three, making nine,
totaling twelve people.
In the Spring and Autumn period, the Son of Heaven took twelve,
a system of the Xià dynasty.
Twenty-seven *shìfù*.
The Yīn people added three times nine again, twenty-seven,
A total of thirty-nine people.
Eighty-one imperial concubines.
The Zhōu 周 dynasty esteemed the methods of Emperor Kù 帝嚳's principal consort.
Moreover, nine times nine equals eighty-one,
adding this to the total makes one hundred and twenty people.
The Son of Heaven takes twelve women,
symbolizing the twelve months.
Three *fū rén* 夫人 and nine *pín* 嬪.
A feudal lord takes nine women,
symbolizing the nine provinces.
One wife and eight concubines.
A high minister (*qīng dà fū* 卿大夫) has one wife and two concubines.
A *shì* 士 (gentleman) has one wife and one concubine.
Differences in the conferred lands of the sons and daughters of kings:
The emperor's daughter is called *gōng zhǔ* 公主 (princess),
with ceremony comparable to that of a feudal lord.
The emperor's elder sister is called *zhǎng gōng zhǔ* 長公主 (grand princess),
with ceremony comparable to that of a feudal king.
Unrelated women bestowed a fief by grace are called *jūn* 君,
comparable to a grand princess.
Distinct names for the ancestral temple of the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords:
The ancestral temple is to the left.
East is called "left."
The emperor's sacrificial animals are kept in pens for three months:
one month in an outer pen,
one month in a middle pen,
one month in a bright pen,
This refers to being near the Mingtang.
After being fed for three months at a time, they are sufficiently fat.
Moving them after three months
is to show their cleanliness.
To the right is the altar to the gods of earth and grain.
West is called right.
Ancestral temples and altars to the gods of earth and grain were all located inside the storehouse gate and outside the pheasant gate.
The Son of Heaven had seven temples: three Zhao, three Mu, and the temple of the great ancestor.
Seven temples, one altar, and one flat altar.
These were called the Temple of the Father, the Temple of the Grandfather, the Temple of the Great-Grandfather, the Temple of the Exalted Grandfather, and the Temple of the Ancestral Grandfather.
All were sacrificed to monthly.
The feudal lords had five temples: two Zhao, two Mu, and the temple of the great ancestor.
Five temples, one altar, and one flat altar.
These were called the Temple of the Father, the Temple of the Grandfather, and the Temple of the Great-Grandfather.
All were sacrificed to monthly.
Different names for the temples below the rank of Daifu:
A Daifu had three temples: one Zhao, one Mu, and the temple of the great ancestor.
Three temples and one altar.
The Temple of the Father and the Temple of the Grandfather were sacrificed to during the four seasons.
A Shi had one temple,
which was a level below the Daifu's two temples.
An Upper Shi had two temples and one altar,
the Temple of the Father and the Temple of the Grandfather.
They were only sacrificed to during the four seasons.
They independently established two sacrifices, one called the Gate and one called the Road.
A Lower Shi had one temple, called the Temple of the Father.
The Grandfather had no temple but was sacrificed to.
What is called "zǔ chēng yuē miào" 祖稱曰廟 refers to the ancestral temple.
Two ancestral shrines are also established,
the same as for senior scholars (shàng shì 上士).
Those below the level of Fǔ Shǐ 府史 who do not have official titles
are called commoners (shù rén 庶人).
Commoners do not have ancestral temples;
instead, they perform the seasonal sacrifices in their bedrooms (qǐn 寢).
In the Zhōu 周 dynasty, Wén Wǔ 文武 were regarded as "tiāo 祧" (referring to ancestral shrines to which sacrifices are made when the main line is not yet full).
They were merely sacrificed to during the four seasons.
When removing the *tiāo* shrine, it becomes an altar (*tán* 壇).
When removing the *tán* altar, it becomes a *shàn* 墠 (a cleared and leveled space for sacrifice).
If there is a prayer (dǎo 禱),
sacrifice to it;
if there is no prayer, then stop.
Removing the *shàn* leveled space results in a *guǐ* 鬼 (ghost).
*Tán* 壇 refers to building a raised earth platform to form a hall.
*Shàn* 墠 refers to building an earth platform without a building on it.
One offers ancestors at the appropriate place of their bedchamber (shì qǐn 適寢).
In spring, one offers chives and eggs;
in summer, wheat and fish;
in autumn, millet and pork;
in winter, rice and goose.
There are no fixed sacrificial animals.
One simply chooses what is appropriate and in season.
The Son of Heaven's (Tiānzǐ 天子) *zōngshè 宗社* (ancestral altar and earth altar) is called *Tài Shè* 泰社,
which the Son of Heaven establishes for all the various clans.
The Son of Heaven's (Tiānzǐ's) altar of the soil is called the Royal Altar (Wángshè),
and is also called the Imperial Altar (Dìshè).
In ancient times, when an order was given to dispatch troops,
the authority was always conferred at this altar.
The *Shangshu* says:
"Those who obey the order are rewarded at the ancestral temple (zǔ),
those who disobey the order are executed at the altar of the soil (shè)."
When feudal lords (zhūhóu) establish altars for the common people, they are called State Altars (Guóshè);
the feudal lords' own altars are called Marquis Altars (Hóushè).
The altar of a vanquished state:
in ancient times, the Son of Heaven would also take the altar of a vanquished state and distribute it to the feudal lords,
causing them to establish it as an altar to warn and admonish themselves,
covering its top with a roof so that it would not communicate with Heaven,
and filling its base with firewood so that it would not communicate with Earth,
thus severing its connection with Heaven and Earth,
facing north toward the shade,
to indicate its extinction.
When Grand Masters (dàfū) and those below establish altars in groups, they are called Settled Altars (Zhìshè);
Grand Masters were not allowed to establish altars individually,
but lived with their ethnic groups,
and common people and above would share one altar together,

according to ritual, brothers do not succeed one another.

The system of ancestral temples:
Ancient scholars believed that the residence of a ruler
had a court in the front
and a sleeping chamber in the rear.
Upon death, a temple was built in the front to resemble the court,
and a chamber was built in the rear to resemble the sleeping chamber.
The temple was used to store the spirit tablet
and arranged in zhaomu order;
the sleeping chamber contained clothing, hats, walking sticks,
and items symbolizing life.
Collectively, these were called the palace.
The *Yuèlìng* says:
"First offer sacrifices in the sleeping chamber of the temple."
The *Shī* says:
"The palace of dukes and marquises."
The *Sòng* says:
"The sleeping chamber of the temple is grand."
The words are connected,
and these are all references to it.
In ancient times, there were no tomb sacrifices.
It was only when Qín Shǐhuáng built sleeping quarters at the side of his tomb
that the Hàn Dynasty followed suit and did not change the practice.
Therefore, today, above the mausoleums, they are called sleeping palaces,
with preparations for daily life, clothing, and symbols of life,
All this follows the intent of the ancient sleeping chambers.
When residing in Xīdū (西都),
from Gāo Dì (高帝) downwards,
each emperor had a separate temple established.
Monthly, ceremonial carriages and robes were prepared and paraded.
Furthermore, the ritual of alternating destruction [of temples] was not yet established.
During the time of Yuán Dì (元帝),
the Chancellor Kuāng Héng (匡衡) and the Imperial Censor Gòng Yǔ (貢禹) then used the meaning of the classics to correct this,
abolishing the parade of ceremonial robes,
and destroying the temples of former emperors whose kinship was exhausted.
Gāo Dì (高帝) was designated Tàizǔ (太祖),
Xiào Wén (孝文) was designated Tàizōng (太宗),
Xiào Wǔ (孝武) was designated Shìzōng (世宗),
Xiào Xuān (孝宣) was designated Zhōngzōng (中宗).
The temples of the ancestors were all offered sacrifices in perpetuity,
while the others, from Huì (惠) and Jǐng (景) downwards, were all destroyed.
Every five years, an Īnjì (殷祭) sacrifice was performed,
which was like the ancient dì (禘) and xiá (祫) sacrifices.
During the Īnjì (殷祭) sacrifice, all the destroyed temples were included;
if it wasn't an Īnjì (殷祭) sacrifice, only the ancestors were included.
When Guāng Wǔ (光武) revived the dynasty,
and established the capital in Luòyáng (洛陽),
he combined the temples of Gāo Zǔ (高祖) downwards to Píng Dì (平帝) into one temple,
housing the spirit tablets of eleven emperors within it.
Yuán Dì (元帝) was Guāng Wǔ's (光武) father's generation (禰),
therefore, although not a direct ancestor, his temple was not destroyed.
Later descendants followed this precedent,
and thus constantly offered sacrifices to Guāng Wǔ (光武), who raised the empire to receive the mandate again and restore the Hàn (漢) lineage.
They further erected a temple called Shìzǔ (世祖).
When Xiàomíng (孝明) was on the verge of death, his posthumous decree instructed them to follow frugality and not build a sleeping temple.
His spirit tablet was to be enshrined in the Shìzǔ (世祖) Temple.
Xiàozhāng (孝章) dared not disobey.
From then on, they followed and enshrined the spirit tablets in the Shìzǔ (世祖) Temple,
all according to the rites of Xiàomíng (孝明);
however, they all separately built sleeping temples at their mausoleums.
Xiàomíng (孝明) was called Xiǎnzōng (顯宗),
Xiàozhāng (孝章) was called Sùzōng (肅宗).
Later emperors followed this precedent.
Xiàohé (孝和) was called Mùzōng (穆宗),
Xiào'ān (孝安) was called Gōngzōng (恭宗),
Xiàoshùn (孝順) was called Jìngzōng (敬宗),
Xiàohuán (孝桓) was called Wēizōng (威宗).
Only the three young emperors, Shāng (殤), Chōng (沖), and Zhì (質),
all died before reaching adulthood.
They were not included in the imperial ancestral temple.
They were only offered sacrifices at their mausoleums during the four seasons at the sleeping temple.
Now, at the various mausoleums in Luòyáng (洛陽),

on the last day of the month (晦), the first day of the month (望), the twenty-four solar terms (二十四氣), the day for agricultural deities (伏), the local god day (社), the winter solstice sacrifice (臘), and the four seasonal days, rice is offered.
The imperial pantry sends the provisions.
The mausoleum director and food supervisor oversee the palace women at their respective emperors' mausoleums,

On the fifth day of the first month, after the emperor completes the offerings, he goes to the original mausoleum,
going through them in order.
The dukes, ministers, and all the officials followed.
The women of the four prominent families (sì xìng), minor marquises (xiǎo hóu), and various feudal lords.
All those related to the late emperor (xiān dì) and empress dowagers (xiān hòu).

Also, the feudal lords (zhū hóu wáng), grand masters (dà fū), tribute officials from the commanderies and kingdoms (jùn guó jì lì), the Xiongnu envoys (xiōng nú cháo zhě), and the attendants from the Western Regions (xī guó shì zǐ) were all present.
Including the staff of the Ministry of Documents (shàng shū guān shǔ).
West of the steps, beneath the platform, was the spirit seat of the late emperor (xiān dì shén zuò).
Later, the grand masters and tribute officials were all placed below the eaves.
The price of grain in their commanderies was reported.
And the disasters and anomalies from the four quarters.
All were intended to be fully heard by the soul and spirit of the late emperor (xiān dì hún shén).
Consequently, each tribute official was given gifts at their respective imperial mausoleums (qīn líng) and sent away.
In the first month, on the day *dīng* (a cyclical day), sacrifices were offered at the southern suburban altar (nán jiāo).
After the ceremony was completed.
They proceeded to the Bright Hall (míng táng) at the northern suburban altar.
The temple of Emperor Gaozu (gāo zǔ miào) and the temple of Emperor Shizu (shì zǔ miào) were called the Five Offerings (wǔ gōng).
After the Five Offerings were completed.
They proceeded to the imperial mausoleums in order.
For the ancestral temples in the four seasons (sì shí zōng miào), eighteen great offerings of oxen (tài láo) were used.
All had secondary sacrificial animals.
The Five Primary Spirits (wǔ zhǔ) in the Western Temple (xī miào) were:
Emperor Gao (gāo dì), Emperor Wen (wén dì), Emperor Wu (wǔ dì), Emperor Xuan (xuān dì), and Emperor Yuan (yuán dì).
Emperor Gao (gāo dì) was Gaozu (gāo zǔ).
Emperor Wen (wén dì) was Taizong (tài zōng).
Emperor Wu (wǔ dì) was Shizong (shì zōng).
Emperor Xuan (xuān dì) was Zhongzong (zhōng zōng).
Their temples were not destroyed.
Emperor Yuan (xiào yuán) had little merit and should have had his temple destroyed.
However, Emperor Guangwu (guāng wǔ) restored the empire.
His collateral younger brother was made a son to Emperor Yuán
and Emperor Yuán was taken as the temple of the father,
thus he was placed among the ancestors.
Later generations continued this,
and consequently it was not destroyed.
The seven ancestral tablets in the eastern temple were for:
Emperor Guāngwǔ, Emperor Míng, Emperor Zhāng, Emperor Hé, Emperor Ān, Emperor Shùn, and Emperor Huán.
Emperor Guāngwǔ was the founder of the dynasty (Shìzǔ),
Emperor Míng was the brilliant ancestor (Xiǎnzōng),
Emperor Zhāng was the solemn ancestor (Sùzōng),
Emperor Hé was the reverent ancestor (Mùzōng),
Emperor Ān was the respectful ancestor (Gōngzōng),
Emperor Shùn was the esteemed ancestor (Jìngzōng),
Emperor Huán was the majestic ancestor (Wēizōng).
Their temples were all not destroyed.
The young emperors who died before reaching their first year
were not placed in the ancestral temple.
There were three cases where the imperial tombs were treated as temples:
Emperor Shāng's Kāng Mausoleum, Emperor Chōng's Huái Mausoleum, and Emperor Zhì's Jìng Mausoleum.
There were three empresses posthumously honored:
Consort Sòng of Emperor Zhāng, called Empress Jìngyǐn,
buried at the Northern Mausoleum;
she was the grandmother of Emperor Ān.
Empress Xiàodé of Qīnghé was the mother of Emperor Ān.
Consort Liáng of Emperor Zhāng, called Empress Gōnghuái,
buried at the Western Mausoleum;
she was the mother of Emperor Hé.
Ān Dì's Zhāng Guìrén was called the Gōngmǐn Empress,
and was buried in the North Mausoleum;
she was the mother of Shùn Dì.
The two temples (of the founding emperors) with twelve principal ancestral tablets, three young emperors, and three empresses,
therefore used the eighteen *tàiláo* sacrifices.
The Hàn dynasty did not speak of *dì* or *xiá* sacrifices;
after every five years, there were two *yīnjì* sacrifices,
then in the Western Temple, Huì Dì, Jǐng, and Zhāo were all worshiped separately.
Chéng, Āi, and Píng three emperors, because they were not descendants of Guāngwǔ,
their ancestral tablets were stored in Cháng'ān.
Therefore, the Gāo Temple had four seasonal sacrifices in the Eastern Temple.
The Jingzhao Magistrate assisted in the sacrifices, providing clothing, hats, carriages, and accessories,
just like the Grand Master of Ceremonies performing the rites for the mausoleums and temples.
The mother of Shùn Dì was said to be surnamed Lǐ,
or perhaps surnamed Zhāng.
When Gāozǔ obtained the empire,
his father was still alive.
He bestowed upon him the honored title of Grand Supreme Emperor (*tàishàng huáng*),
not calling him "emperor,"
for he was not the Son of Heaven.
Xiào Xuān inherited from Xiào Zhāo Dì;
his father was called the Grandson of the Emperor Shǐ,
and his grandfather was called the Crown Prince Wèi.
The Crown Prince was deposed for a crime,
and both the Crown Prince and the Imperial Grandson died.
Xuān Dì only established a garden and mausoleum with caretakers to maintain and guard it;
he did not dare to bestow an honored title upon his grandfather.
After Guāngwǔ 光武 succeeded Xiàoyuán 孝元,
he also did not dare to bestow honorary titles upon his father and grandfather.
Emperor Shìzǔ's 世祖 father, the Lord of Nándùn 南頓, was called "Imperial Father" (Huáng kǎo 皇考),
his grandfather, the Commandant of Jùlù 鉅鹿, was called "Imperial Grandfather" (Huáng zǔ 皇祖),
and his great-grandfather, the Grand Administrator of Yùlín 鬱林, was called "Imperial Great-Grandfather" (Huáng zēng zǔ 皇曾祖).
His great-great-grandfather, the Marquis of Chōnglíng 舂陵, was called "Imperial Great-Great-Grandfather" (Huáng gāo zǔ 皇高祖).
He erected a mausoleum and temple,
and established Zhānglíng 章陵 to offer sacrifices to them, nothing more.
When Emperor Shāng 殤 died,
without sons or brothers,
Emperor Ān 安, as the son of Emperor Hé's 和 older brother, succeeding from the Prince of Qīnghé 清河, bestowed an honorary title,
following the example of Emperor Gāo 高 honoring his father as the Supreme Emperor (Tàishàng Huáng 太上皇),
posthumously honoring his father, the King of Qīnghé 清河, as Emperor Xiàodé 孝德.
When Emperor Shùn 順 died,
Emperor Chōng 沖 had no sons or brothers,
and the Prince of Lè'ān 樂安 was established,
becoming Emperor Zhì 質.
The emperor, pressured by the father of Empress Liáng 梁 of Emperor Shùn 順, the Grand General Liáng Jì 梁冀, died before he could honor his father.
Emperor Huán 桓, succeeding to the throne as the son of the Marquis of Lǐwú 蠡吾,
posthumously honored his father, the late Marquis of Lǐwú 蠡吾, as Emperor Xiàochóng 孝崇,
his mother, Lady Kuāng 匡, as Empress Xiàochóng 孝崇,
his grandfather, the King of Héjiān 孝河間, as Emperor Xiàomù 孝穆,
and his grandmother, the Consort, as Empress Xiàomù 孝穆.
When Emperor Huán 桓 died,
without sons,
the current Emperor ascended the throne,
posthumously honoring his father, the Marquis of Jiědú 解犢, as Emperor Xiàorén 孝仁,
his mother, Lady Dǒng 董, as Empress Xiàorén 孝仁,
My grandfather, the Jìng King of Héjiān, was called Xiàoyuán Emperor;
my grandmother, Consort Xià, was called Xiàoyuán Empress.
At the grand ancestral altar of the Son of Heaven,
a platform was made of five-colored earth.
When an imperial son was enfeoffed as a king,
he received earth from the ancestral altar of the Son of Heaven in the color corresponding to the direction of his fief:
the east received blue,
the south received red,
and so on for the other directions, according to their respective colors.
It was wrapped with white *mao* grass and bestowed upon him,
each according to the color of the direction of his fief.
He returned to his state to establish an ancestral altar,
hence it was called receiving *mao* earth.
From the rise of the Hàn dynasty, imperial sons enfeoffed as kings received *mao* earth.
Meritorious officials and commoner marquises of other surnames in townships and villages within their territory
each had their household tax revenue limited by number,
and did not receive *mao* earth,
nor did they establish ancestral altars.
According to the Hàn system,
imperial sons enfeoffed as kings
were in reality like the feudal lords of antiquity.
Towards the end of the Zhōu dynasty, some feudal lords called themselves kings,
but the Hàn Son of Heaven referred to himself as emperor,
therefore the title of king was added to them,
collectively naming the feudal lords, princes, and younger brothers.
Those enfeoffed as marquises
These were called Zhūhóu [諸侯].
Those among the assembled officials who had different surnames and were enfeoffed for their merit
were called Chèhóu [徹侯].
Later, to avoid the taboo name of Emperor Wǔdì [武帝], the name was changed to Tōnghóu [通侯].
Legal scholars all called them Lièhóu [列侯].
Those whose merit and virtue were particularly outstanding and were distinguished by the imperial court
were granted the rank of Tèjìn [特進],
whose rank was below the Three Dukes (Sāngōng [三公]).
Next were the Cháohóu [朝侯],
whose rank was below the Nine Ministers (Jiǔqīng [九卿]),
all wearing Píngmiǎn [平冕] caps and embroidered clothing,
attending sacrifices at the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
and were called Shìcíhóu [侍祠侯].
Next were the lower-ranked scholars (Xiàshì [下士]),
who only attended sacrifices but had no court position.
Next were the lords of small states (Xiǎoguó hóu [小國侯]),
who were descendants of close relatives and princesses, guarding the tombs,
those in the capital would also attend assemblies from time to time,
and were called Wěicháohóu [猥朝侯].
When the imperial tour and hunting were over,
the dukes and ministers and below would line up on the street in front of the Dūtíng [都亭] in Luoyang [洛陽].
When the imperial carriage arrived,
the dukes and ministers would bow down,
and the Son of Heaven would descend from the carriage.
The dukes and ministers would be recognized and acknowledged,
and then the emperor would return to the palace.
An ancient saying goes:
"[Zài chē zé xià.]
Only at this time is it implemented.
During the New Year's court audience in the first month,
the Three Dukes (Sāngōng) present jade disks (bì) to the palace hall,
facing north towards the imperial throne.
The Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng) intones:
"The Emperor rises for you, my lords,
the Three Dukes prostrate themselves,
the Emperor sits,
and then the jade disks are presented."
An ancient saying goes:
"When the Emperor sits on his throne, then rise."
This is what it refers to.
According to the old rituals, officials below the Three Dukes had monthly court audiences,
but these were later reduced.
It was customary to hold court audiences on the first day of the sixth month and the first day of the tenth month.
Later, the sixth-month audience was also omitted due to the intense heat.
Therefore, now only the first month and tenth month audiences are held.
At the winter solstice, the yang qi (yáng qì) begins to stir,
and at the summer solstice, the yin qi (yīn qì) begins to rise.
The elk and deer shed their antlers.
Therefore, the war drums are silenced.
The body should desire tranquility,
and the mind should desire quietude.
No affairs are heard.
Welcoming and sending off (the seasons) lasts for five days.
The Là sacrifice is a great year-end sacrifice.
When officials and commoners held feasts and drinking parties,
it was not to welcome the arrival of seasonal Qi,
therefore they only saw it off but did not welcome it.
The beginning of the year in the first month
was also like the rituals of the Là sacrifice.
At the Winter Solstice, the Yáng Qì arises,
the way of the ruler grows,
therefore congratulations are offered.
At the Summer Solstice, the Yīn Qì arises,
the way of the ruler declines,
therefore no congratulations are offered.
Drums are used to mobilize the masses,
bells are used to stop the masses.
When the night water clock is exhausted,
the drum sounds and people rise.
When the day water clock is exhausted,
the bell sounds and people rest.
When the Son of Heaven goes out,
the order of the carriages is called the Lǔbù:
there is the Grand Procession, the Small Procession, and the Ceremonial Procession.
In the Grand Procession, dukes and ministers respectfully lead the way, the Grand General is the co-driver, and the Tàipú is the charioteer,
with eighty-one subordinate carriages,
prepared with a thousand chariots and ten thousand horsemen.
When in Cháng'ān,
to go out to sacrifice to Heaven at Gānquán, it was fully prepared,
and the hundred officials had their ritual annotations,
called the Gānquán Lǔbù.
Since the Restoration (Zhōngxīng), it has rarely been used.
During the time of the late emperor,
when preparing the grand procession to Yuánlíng,

Only upon encountering great funerals
was the imperial procession (fǎjià) employed.
The high officials and ministers were not included in the imperial retinue (lǔbù).

For the Northern Suburban Sacrifice (Běi Jiāo) and the Bright Hall (Míngtáng),
the various secondary carriages were reduced.
The lesser procession (xiǎojià) was used for sacrifices to the ancestral temples.
Each time [the procession] went out,

The spring and autumn imperial visits to the mausoleums further reduced the scale compared to the lesser procession (xiǎojià).
A single directing secretary of the Ministry of Affairs (Zhíshì Shàngshū) and those below would proceed in advance.
In the imperial procession (fǎjià), the vehicle the emperor rode in was called the Golden Root Carriage (Jīngēnchē).
It was drawn by six horses,
of five colors.
The comfort carriages (ānchē) were of five colors,
and the standing carriages (lìchē) each of one color.
All were drawn by four horses,
these served as the secondary carriages for the five seasons.
Common people called them the Five Emperor Carriages (Wǔdìchē),
but this was incorrect.
There was also a military standing carriage (róng lìchē) for military expeditions.
The three-covered carriage was called the Ploughing Root Carriage (Gēnggēnchē),
One is called the Zhī Chē (芝車),
which the emperor uses when personally plowing the Jì Tián (耤田).
There is also the Tà Zhū Chē (蹋豬車),
with painted designs on the awning wheel.
He rides this when hunting.
A green carriage is called the Huángsūn Chē (皇孫車),
which the emperor's grandsons ride
to follow.
All royal carriages have a feathered canopy, golden Huá Guā (華瓜),
a yellow awning, a left Dào (纛),
golden Zōng (鍐), square Xì (釳),
elaborate tassels, double hubs, and extra towing.
The yellow awning means the canopy is lined with yellow.
The left Dào (纛) is made of yak tail,
and is as large as a Dǒu (斗).
It is located on the left flank horse's mane in the rear.
The golden Zōng (鍐) is a horse's crown,
with a height and width of four Cùn (寸) each,
in the shape of a jade flower,
and is located in front of the horse's mane.
The square Xì (釳) is
several Cùn (寸) of iron in width,
and is behind the mane,
with three holes
to insert pheasant tails into.
Elaborate tassels are in front of the horse's chest,
like a skirt of ropes.

Linchpins are applied to the exterior,

The gilded bronze decorations are shaped like orange silk;
the axle caps are cushioned with oily orange silk,
eight inches wide
and long enough to reach the ground.
A blue dragon is painted on the left,
and a white tiger on the right.
It is attached to the axle head.
Carriages for officials earning two thousand *dàn* of grain are similar today,
except without the paintings.
The vanguard consists of nine-streamer banners with cloud patterns, halberds with butts, leather-covered carriages and carriages with bell flags.
All the carriages carry the bell flags for the high-ranking officials;
feathers are woven and tied alongside the pole.
Common people call them "chicken-feather carriages,"
which is incorrect.
Behind them are carriages bearing gilded bells, yellow battleaxes, and the yellow-gate drums.
In ancient times, feudal lords had nine duplicate chariots.
When the Qin dynasty conquered the nine kingdoms, it annexed their carriages and attire.
Therefore, the imperial grand procession included eighty-one attached carriages.
The Masters of Writing and Imperial Scribes ride in them.
The last carriage has a leopard tail hanging from it,
while all the preceding carriages are leather-covered, made with tiger skin.
In the seventh year of the Yǒng'ān era
Jiàn Jīngēn and Gēnggēn, along with other imperial carriages,
all had a single shaft,
some with four horses,
some with six horses.
The boxes and wheels of the Jīngēn carriage were all decorated with gold of a pure yellow color.
Both arms (of the carriage) were engraved with gold at the front and back,
creating the shapes of dragons, tigers, birds, and turtles.
The top was simply covered with blue silk,
and there were no doors at the back adorned with feathers.
Mǎn Guān (ceremonial headdress):
In the Zhōu dynasty, it was called juébìan;
In the Yīn dynasty, it was called xǔ;
In the Xià dynasty, it was called shōu.
All used thirty shēng of lacquered cloth to make the shell,
with a width of eight cùn,
and a length of one chǐ and two cùn.
A jué miǎn (a type of crown) was added on top.
The Zhōu dynasty's version was black with red,
the color of a sparrow's head.
It was smaller in the front and larger in the back.
The Yīn dynasty's version was black with a hint of white.
It was larger in the front and smaller in the back.
The Xià dynasty's version was purely black with red.
